In the developing retina, neural progenitor cells undergo vertical nuclear migration between the ventricular and marginal zones, occurring between cell divisions. This study investigates the dynamics of nuclear movement in retinal progenitors from early stages of zebrafish eye development. By analyzing the positions of nuclei within the developing retina, researchers found that the movement of nuclei follows a pattern consistent with Brownian motion. This study reveals that the diffusion coefficient of nuclei is influenced by the stage of development and the location within the retina, with nuclei in the ventricular zone experiencing higher resistance than those in the marginal zone. This study also suggests that cytoskeletal components may play a role in regulating nuclear movement, with nuclei in the ventricular zone experiencing higher resistance than those in the marginal zone. This study provides insights into the mechanisms underlying retinal development and the role of cytoskeletal components in regulating nuclear movement.

In various image and video processing tasks, such as demosaicing and compressive video reconstruction, code-based methods have achieved remarkable success. To take these techniques to the next level, we introduce a novel code optimization framework that leverages perceptual loss functions. This approach allows us to incorporate human visual system characteristics into the design of optimized codes, resulting in improved performance in downstream applications. Our method is particularly effective in video reconstruction, where we demonstrate that our codes outperform existing approaches in terms of both visual and quantitative metrics.

The behavior of active matter systems with inactive structural defects has not been extensively studied, despite their relevance in various active contexts. This study investigates the dynamics of active fluids with quenched disorder in dimensions greater than two dimensions, using a model of incompressible polar active fluid with pressure-driven flow around inactive obstacles. The system exhibits a distinct phase transition, characterized by a sudden change in the pressure difference across the system, which can be described using the concept of marginal relevance. The critical behavior of the system is found to be independent of the specific details of active forces, and the critical exponents are consistent with those of the 3D Ising model. The study also reveals that the system exhibits a non-trivial relationship between the pressure difference and the activity, which can be described using the concept of marginal relevance.

Researchers in computer science often work in networks, and their research areas are frequently interconnected. To uncover hidden research topics within these networks, we developed a new approach that combines network dynamics with network representation learning. Our method, called Dynamic Temporal Attention Network Embedding (DTANE), can track the evolution of research topics over time and identify previously overlooked areas. We applied DTANE to analyze the co-authorship network of the SIGKDD community, and it successfully identified vulnerable research areas and overlooked topics.

Recent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy studies have discovered a unique pseudogap feature in copper-oxide superconductors, characterized by an elliptical contour that contracts as doping increases, converging on the antiferromagnetic van Hove edge of the electronic band structure. This edge, located near the anti-nodal point, has been associated with the onset of superconductivity. We demonstrate that this edge can be eliminated through lattice strain, causing the pseudogap contour to shift inward, away from the Fermi energy. This finding suggests that the contour is not defined by the edge's location, but rather by an additional feature within the electron-filled Brillouin zone. We propose that this feature is a saddle point that emerges from hybridization between electrons and spin fluctuations, and we show that it can be understood through a minimal model of interacting electrons.

A novel device has been created to collect spallation neutrons at the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory, located 100 meters underground in Scotland. This device consists of a 1-meter long, 10-centimeter diameter tube made of paraffin wax, positioned horizontally within a 1-meter long, 10-centimeter diameter lead tube. The paraffin tube is lined with 1000 3-inch NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors, which are used to measure neutron capture gamma rays. The device operates by detecting gamma rays with energies between 300 and 400 keV, which are emitted when a thermal neutron interacts with an iodine nucleus. The device's design and performance are described in detail, along with the results of a live measurement of the spallation neutron flux, which are presented in the associated research paper.

This paper investigates the normalized ground states of a biharmonic Choquard equation with a term exhibiting exponential growth, subject to a specific constraint. By applying variational methods and concentration compactness principles, we establish the existence of normalized ground states under certain conditions.

The next few years will see a significant increase in the number of exoplanets discovered thanks to the synergy of the TESS and Kepler missions, which will likely yield thousands of new exoplanets, including high-priority targets for future research. To complement this, the TESS-Keck Study aims to take advantage of the capabilities of the Keck I/II telescopes and their high-resolution spectrographs to study the atmospheres of these exoplanets. By utilizing the capabilities of these instruments, the study will use the radial velocity method to precisely measure the masses of these exoplanets, as well as the chemical composition of their host stars, which will help to interpret the transmission spectra obtained from the TESS and Kepler missions. To achieve these goals, the study has developed a rigorous methodology for selecting a diverse sample of exoplanets that span a wide range of characteristics, including their masses, sizes, and orbital periods. By using this methodology, the study has identified a target list of approximately 1000 exoplanets that are expected to be discovered in the coming years, which will be prioritized for follow-up observations.

This research focuses on developing an Indonesian ID card extraction tool that leverages optical character recognition (OCR) and natural language processing (NLP) to automate the retrieval of personal information from ID cards. By utilizing NLP, the study aims to enhance the accuracy of OCR by correcting any errors in the recognized text. The proposed method employs Tesseract 5 for OCR and the spaCy NLP library for natural language processing. The results indicate that the combination of OCR and NLP significantly improves the accuracy of ID card data extraction, achieving a retrieval F1 score of 0.99.

A quantum harmonic oscillator's imaginary time path integral was numerically calculated in the presence of a constant external force, with results showing excellent agreement with established analytical solutions.

This study investigates the YORP effect's influence on three asteroids: 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro. By analyzing light curve data from various sources, we determined their rotation periods and used a 3D model to estimate the YORP acceleration based on their physical properties. Our findings show that the YORP effect is accelerating 1992 SK's rotation at a rate of 1.05 x 10^-9 rad/s/s, while it is decelerating Geographos and Toro at rates of 1.10 x 10^-9 rad/s/s and 1.00 x 10^-9 rad/s/s, respectively.

This study examines the conversational interactions among political figures on Instagram, utilizing network analysis to investigate the spread of ideas and opinions within social media discussions. By leveraging the retweet network, we investigate the spread of ideas and opinions within social media discussions. Initially, we investigate the structural characteristics of the retweet network, including its degree distribution, community organization, and temporal evolution. Subsequently, we employ topic modeling to investigate the content of conversations and their evolution over time. By integrating this content analysis with node centrality metrics, we identify key influencers within specific topics and explore how their opinions shape the broader discussion. Our findings reveal that political figures who engage in discussions with a broad range of other politicians tend to have a greater impact on the broader discussion. Additionally, we find that politicians who interact with a diverse range of other politicians tend to have a greater influence on the broader discussion.

We demonstrate that any compact collection of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms mapping the unit disk to itself, with derivative behavior at the origin that is uniformly bounded, includes a homeomorphism whose derivative at the origin cannot be bounded by any uniform limit.

This study examines 100 low-mass stars with K-band magnitudes between 8 and 14, which were previously identified as single by the Gaia DR3 astrometry. By analyzing their optical spectra, we determined their effective temperatures, surface gravities, and metal abundances, and found that 60 of these stars are likely single, while 40 may be part of binary systems. We also found that the sample contains both young and old stars, and that the fraction of binaries increases with age. Our analysis also revealed that the sample contains stars with a wide range of rotation periods, which can be used to estimate stellar ages. We found that the sample contains both rapidly rotating young stars and slowly rotating old stars, and that the rotation period distribution is consistent with that of other low-mass star samples. We also found that the sample contains stars with a wide range of X-ray luminosities, which can be used to estimate stellar ages. We found that the sample contains both X-ray bright young stars and X-ray dim old stars, and that the X-ray luminosity distribution is consistent with that of other low-mass star samples. We also found that the sample contains stars with a wide range of chromospheric activity levels, which can be used to estimate stellar ages. We found that the sample contains both highly active young stars and inactive old stars, and that the chromospheric activity level distribution is consistent with that of other low-mass star samples.

We have engineered a novel type of material called a dual metasurface, which can interact with line-shaped ripples in a unique way. By modifying the ripple's orientation, this material allows for precise control over how the ripples scatter. Our design leverages a specific type of electromagnetic response, enabling the dual metasurface to achieve this line-ripple control. We have demonstrated this concept with a prototype made of silicon, which shows that our surface can effectively change how line-ripples scatter.

The complexity of evaluating first-order database queries has been extensively researched, with the focus on acyclic queries and their subcategories. This paper builds upon the work of previous studies by analyzing the data complexity of 3-variable acyclic conjunctive queries, with an aim to understand how the structure of the query's dependency graph affects evaluation. Specifically, we investigate the impact of self-loops on the evaluation of 3-variable acyclic conjunctive queries. We demonstrate that the evaluation of such queries is solvable in logarithmic time with respect to database size, with an associated randomized space of logarithmic space. Moreover, we show that this evaluation problem is complete for NL under randomized reductions, thus confirming its non-P status. This result is in contrast to the evaluation of 3-variable acyclic conjunctive queries without self-loops, which are all equivalent to evaluating boolean 3-CNF formulas.

The concept of regularity is fundamental to the study of infinite words and has been extensively studied using various formalisms, including automata, MSO logic, and rational power series. The regularity of an object can be verified by demonstrating that it matches a specific, pre-defined description. In this study, we explore the class of rational power series and identify a subclass that can be characterized by its equivalence to regular MSO formulas over infinite words. We also provide a characterization of this subclass using two additional formalisms, and we prove that these formalisms are aligned with the Büchi-Mazet theorem for co-Büchi automata with parity acceptance conditions. We further establish that the parity condition can be eliminated from this formalism, and we prove that this characterization is equivalent to a specific class of rational power series that can be described using a third formalism.

This paper presents amplitude analyses for the $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ and $B_{(s)} \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decays, and reports the first measurement of the $B \to K^{*0} \overline{K}^{*0}$ decay's branching fraction.

In complex dynamical systems, multiple coexisting basins of attraction can exist within the same parameter space. These basins represent regions where initial conditions lead to the same long-term behavior. Identifying these hidden basins is crucial for understanding and controlling such systems. A novel method has been developed to map these basins by utilizing a dynamic control parameter and a specific algorithm. This approach involves varying the control parameter in a controlled manner and using a distance metric to detect the system's behavior. The results show that this method can reveal previously unknown coexisting attractors in a range of complex dynamical systems, including a R\"ossler system, a Chua circuit, and a Lorenz system.

This paper introduces novel unbiased estimators for mean absolute deviation around the median in both population and regression contexts. To achieve this, we employ combinatorial methods to calculate exact sampling distributions of the MAD estimator, allowing for precise computation of unbiased estimates through moment calculations. Our analysis includes exact sampling distributions for various scenarios, including simple random sampling, i.i.d., and i.i.d. normal data. To extend our findings to i.f.r. normal data, we develop an exact finite sample distribution for the scaled MAD estimator, facilitating accurate computation of its unbiased version. Additionally, we employ a Bahadur-type representation to derive the asymptotic normality of the MAD estimator, enabling the calculation of variance and standard error estimates via the delta method. Our simulation studies demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed estimators in practice.

This study proposes a novel method for approximating second-order reachable sets by utilizing a variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation of the Cauchy type. The underlying rationale is that the set of states reachable from any given state can be determined by solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, whose solution provides the minimum time required to reach a target set. To solve this equation, we employ a discrete approach based on the Lax-Friedrichs scheme, which is shown to converge to the exact solution under specific conditions. The convergence proof is provided, and the resulting method offers an efficient and accurate way to calculate reachable sets.

Local functional illustrations are a category of neural network architectures
that have been extensively utilized in diverse applications, such as
machine learning and medical imaging, to identify and classify objects within
a specific image. These models typically employ a two-step process, where a
neural network activates a limited number of regions within an image, and a
classifier then uses these activated areas to make a decision. However,
previous methods often require a significant amount of training data to
achieve satisfactory results, and they may struggle to generalize well to
unseen scenarios. In this study, we propose a novel approach called MPA (Modulated
Periodic Activations) that automates the activation process and eliminates
the need for a separate classifier. MPA utilizes a neural network to activate
a set of pre-defined, regularly spaced regions within an image, and leverages
the inherent information contained in these activated areas to make a
classification. We demonstrate that MPA outperforms existing methods in
terms of accuracy and generalizability on a variety of datasets, including
MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10. Our approach provides a simple yet effective
solution to the problem of object classification, and it has the potential to
be applied to a wide range of domains.

The brain's neural networks are organized into functional groups that share similar characteristics, and this arrangement is crucial for understanding how the brain works. Research has shown that the ventral temporal cortex, a key area for processing visual information, contains distinct regions that respond to different types of animate objects. However, the underlying structure of this animacy-related response pattern has not been fully understood. Our study reveals that the neural response map in the ventral temporal cortex is essentially a low-dimensional curved surface, which can be described using a mathematical concept called a Riemannian manifold. By applying advanced analytical techniques, we discovered that this curved surface is divided into two distinct areas, each corresponding to animate and inanimate objects. This finding provides a deeper understanding of how the brain's neural networks are organized to process visual information and animacy-related concepts.

We establish the quantum unique ergodicity (QUE) conjecture for Davenport-Heilbergh orthogonality, asserting that the $L^\infty$-norm of Hecke-Maass newforms $f(t)$ scales as $O(t^\varepsilon)$, and this bound holds for all but at most $O(t^\delta)$ possible Landau-Siegel zeros, and we achieve this result with an improved bound for the exceptional zeros, and our approach relies on a novel application of the large sieve to obtain a substantial saving in the second moment of $f(p^n)$ over short intervals of the prime powers, and this method also yields a novel application of the large sieve to the second moment of Hecke-Maass newforms over short intervals of the prime powers, and we further apply this technique to a novel approach to a quantum unique ergodicity for Dirichlet L-functions.

We have developed a quantum relational Hoare logic that incorporates size-change and expectations, which enables inductive proofs and modular reasoning. Our work builds on an existing classical framework, extending it to handle expectations in both post-states and intermediate states in quantum programs. We have also provided a proof of correspondence for our logic, as well as a proof of modularity based on a quantum version of weakest relational precondition.

The transmission of infectious diseases can be significantly influenced by a limited number of highly active individuals known as super-spreaders. This research aims to quantify the role of super-spreader events in various models of disease transmission. We compare two models: one that accounts for large-scale transmission events and another that does not. Our findings reveal that in certain scenarios, a considerable proportion of infections can be attributed to super-spreader events, and this proportion can vary widely depending on the specific situation. The impact of these events is particularly pronounced in the early stages of an epidemic, and it is also affected by factors such as the basic reproduction number and the distribution of transmission events. Our results highlight the importance of identifying and containing super-spreader events in the control of epidemics.

Let G be a group acting on the set X, which consists of linear operators from a complex topological vector space V to itself. This paper investigates the conditions under which X contains a cyclic element that generates a subgroup isomorphic to the entire group G.

Vector magnetic field measurements for the Sun are obtained through the inversion of non-linear radiative transfer equations, which can be influenced by various physical phenomena. These measurements are crucial for understanding solar activity and space weather, but their accuracy is compromised by biases that arise from the assumptions made during the inversion process. In this study, we explore the sources of these biases and their effects on the measurements, and we propose a method to quantify and correct for them. By comparing our results with a range of synthetic and observational data, we demonstrate that our approach can accurately identify and correct for biases that arise from various inversion methods. We also show that our method can be used to improve the reliability of these measurements and to better interpret their implications for solar activity and space weather.

We have developed a method to measure the radii of young stellar clusters in galaxies using photometric data, which involves analyzing the brightness profiles of the clusters and determining the point where they blend into the surrounding stellar populations. We applied this technique to 109 clusters in 10 galaxies, including M31, M33, NGC 6946, and several others, utilizing existing and new data from surveys such as ATLAS3, ATLAS, ATLAS-3D, and ATLAS-A. We found that the radii of these clusters range from 10 to 100 parsecs, with an average of about 40 parsecs, and that the distribution of radii is similar across different galaxies. We also discovered that the radii of these clusters are not significantly influenced by their distance, luminosity, or the properties of their host galaxies, but may be related to the presence of spiral arms. Our results provide valuable insights into the structure and evolution of star-forming regions in galaxies and can inform future studies of galaxy evolution using upcoming surveys such as ATLAS-2D and ATLAS-A.

We have developed a new approach to calculate the decay width of $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$ using lattice QCD, by directly determining the decay amplitude through correlation functions of electromagnetic currents. This method allows us to obtain a precise result, yielding a $\Gamma(\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma)$ value of $6.96(12)_{\rm stat}(10)_{\rm syst}$ keV.

The Hubbard model, a fundamental theoretical framework for describing interacting electrons in a lattice, is extensively studied in condensed matter physics.  However, simulations of the model using quantum Monte Carlo methods are hindered by a sign problem that arises in certain scenarios, making calculations extremely time-consuming.  This study presents a novel approach to mitigating the sign problem by employing a complex-valued neural network that can accurately model the Monte Carlo weight's behavior.  By training the network to mimic the distribution of the weight, we can generate weighted samples that reduce the impact of the sign problem.  Our results demonstrate a significant improvement in computational efficiency, with up to a 100-fold reduction in CPU time required to obtain reliable data.  This approach is particularly effective at low temperatures and large system sizes, where the sign problem is most severe.  Furthermore, our method enables the recovery of key physical quantities, such as the double occupancy and the static susceptibility, with high accuracy.  This study paves the way for more efficient simulations of quantum systems that were previously hindered by the sign problem.

We introduce a novel concept, fragile integers, and examine their frequency within the first $x$ positive integers, denoted as $\pi_{\rm f}(x)/x$. Our analysis reveals that this proportion behaves similarly to $\rho(\log_2 x)$, where $\rho$ is the Dickman function. Furthermore, we explore how this relates to the distribution of binary digits in integers, specifically the proportion of integers with an unusually high or low number of ones in their binary representation.

This paper investigates the topological entropy and factor complexity of continuous functions on the Cantor set and free group automorphisms. We establish upper and lower bounds for the factor complexity and topological entropy when considering compositions of functions and changes in free group bases. Specifically, we prove that the topological entropy of a composed function is bounded by the product of the complexities of the individual functions, and that this bound can be tight. We also show that the topological entropy of a free group automorphism is invariant under basis changes, and that this invariance holds for both rational and non-rational entropies.

In the realm of multi-task learning, models are capable of acquiring knowledge across various related tasks, yet in practical applications, it's often necessary to introduce new tasks without retraining the model. To tackle this challenge, we introduce an innovative unsupervised cross-task generalization framework that leverages the model's ability to transfer knowledge to unfamiliar tasks through retrieval enhancement. Our approach involves pre-training a model on a set of known tasks and subsequently using it to perform clustering on data from an unseen task. By fine-tuning the model's embedding space to optimize task-specific labels, we can generate accurate labels for the data and assign it to the closest known task. Notably, our method does not require any labeled data from the unseen task and can be easily applied to a wide range of tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving impressive cross-task generalization performance on multiple datasets.

This paper introduces a new method for fast autonomous component analysis,
which is a type of self-supervised learning that enables a robot to learn about
its body structure without any external guidance. The proposed method is based
on a new optimization framework that is computationally efficient and can be
implemented in real-time using a mobile robot. The framework is designed to
minimize the difference between a model of the robot's structure and actual
sensor data, which is collected using a depth camera. The method is tested on a
mobile robot with a Kinova Gen3 arm, which has 6 degrees of freedom, and the
results show that the proposed method is able to accurately identify all of the
robot's components in real-time, even when the robot is moving and the camera
is not perfectly aligned with the robot's structure.

This study examines the requirements engineering field within the gaming industry,
which has experienced significant growth in recent years. We investigated current
practices in this sector through a comprehensive analysis of 30 academic and
industry-related studies. Our findings reveal a lack of research focusing on
requirements engineering in the gaming industry, with most existing studies being
project-based and lacking a systematic methodology. We also identified several
key differences between the gaming and other software industries, including
variations in stakeholder involvement, project management approaches, and
product development cycles. We propose a set of research questions and potential
solutions tailored to the gaming industry, which could serve as a foundation for
further investigation.

Optimizing hyperparameters in machine learning models is a crucial yet time-consuming task. This task becomes even more critical in the context of private deep learning, where hyperparameters include not only standard parameters like learning rates and network sizes, but also the privacy budget epsilon and the noise scale delta. In this paper, we investigate the hyperparameter optimization problem for private deep learning models, specifically focusing on the stochastic gradient descent with noise (SGD) algorithm. We propose a novel hyperparameter optimization framework that leverages Bayesian optimization to efficiently identify the optimal hyperparameters. Our framework is designed to handle the complex and high-dimensional search space of private deep learning models, and it incorporates a novel acquisition function that takes into account the differential privacy constraints. We evaluate our framework on two real-world datasets, and we demonstrate that it outperforms existing hyperparameter optimization methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Our results show that our framework can significantly improve the performance of private deep learning models, and it can be easily adapted to other deep learning models and applications.

This study explores the structural composition of involutions within the symmetric group $S_n$ as a Boolean lattice, mirroring a previous lattice study by S. C. Milne. We've identified and classified the structural components of $S_n$ involutions, focusing on modular elements, local lattices, and irreducible components. Notably, we found that the lattice can be broken down into specific components, with each component corresponding to a particular set of disjoint cycles within the involutions.

The Euclid satellite's Narrow-Field Instrument (NISP) will have a significant impact on the scientific knowledge of the universe by the end of this decade. As part of this instrument, the Near-Infrared Spectrometer, will enable the study of the expansion and growth of the universe through a large-scale spectroscopic survey. This research assesses the potential biases in spectroscopic data that could affect the accuracy of the survey's results. A key source of noise in the readout of the instrument's spectrometer is being analyzed to determine its impact on the measurement of the brightness of celestial objects. A detailed simulation of the instrument's performance is used to evaluate the effects of this noise on the data. The results show that the noise can lead to an overestimation of the object's brightness, with the magnitude of the bias depending on the object's actual brightness. The research also proposes a method to correct for this effect, which can be applied to the data to improve the accuracy of the measurements.

We have developed a new approach to chemical cartography, utilizing a large dataset from the APOGEE survey, which consists of 14,000 high-resolution stellar spectra. This dataset allows us to analyze the composition of stars in the Milky Way disk, which are metal-rich and have a wide range of temperatures. We have created two distinct models to determine the composition of these stars, which are then compared to the APOGEE data. This allows us to identify discrepancies between the two models and understand the limitations of each. We have found that our initial model is effective at determining the metal content of stars, but struggles to accurately determine their alpha-element content. Our second model, which utilizes a more complex set of parameters, is able to accurately determine the alpha-element content of stars, but is less effective at determining their metal content. We have also found that the discrepancies between the two models can be used to identify the effects of stellar rotation and other physical phenomena on the composition of stars. This has led us to develop a new approach to understanding the evolution of the Milky Way disk, which is based on the comparison of two distinct models and the analysis of their differences.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to widespread panic and the rapid dissemination of online rumors, posing a significant threat to public health and social stability. This study focuses on measuring the spread and influence of online rumors during the pandemic, using a dataset of 10,000 Weibo posts related to Wuhan. By analyzing the network structure of these posts, we identified key indicators of rumor propagation, including the number of sub-communities, average community size, and the proportion of users who reposted the rumors. We also developed a scoring system to rank the spread and influence of different rumors, and found that certain topics, such as Wuhan's lockdown and medical supply shortages, were more likely to spread rapidly and have a significant impact. This study provides valuable insights for government authorities to effectively manage online information and prevent the dissemination of false information during public health crises.

We have created a comprehensive catalog of 1,144 planetary nebulae across 10 galaxies within the Fornax cluster, utilizing the data from the Fornax3D project. This project has obtained high-resolution spectra for these PNe, allowing us to determine their distances using the method of PN-H$\beta$ Tully-Fisher. By analyzing the expansion velocities of the nebulae, we were able to calculate the distances to each galaxy, resulting in estimates for 10 galaxies within the Fornax cluster. Our results show that our distance estimates are in good agreement with other methods, such as those based on globular clusters and red giant branch stars. Furthermore, our data can be used to study the evolution of planetary nebulae across different environments, as well as the formation of galaxies and their interactions with the surrounding environment.

Periodic data streams, which are commonly found in various fields such as finance, healthcare, and IoT, are characterized by their regular sampling intervals.  These periodic streams are typically processed in batches, but this approach can lead to significant data loss and increased processing times.  To address this issue, we present LifeStream, a high-performance flow processing engine that allows periodic streams to be processed in real-time.  LifeStream is designed to handle multiple stream operations, including filtering, aggregation, and join, and it features a novel scheduling algorithm that optimizes the processing of multiple periodic streams.  Our evaluation results demonstrate that LifeStream outperforms existing batch processing systems and achieves up to a 10x improvement in performance compared to existing stream processing systems.

This research paper focuses on specific types of curves in a given space, namely Bertrand curves and their subcategory, Bertrand-Pfeffer curves. We first establish the conditions for a curve to be classified as a timelike Bertrand curve within the provided space, and then derive similar conditions for timelike Bertrand-Pfeffer curves. Additionally, we illustrate these concepts with two examples.

In classification tasks, selecting an appropriate loss function is a critical step in designing a deep learning model. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the impact of different loss functions on a model's performance. To achieve this, we conducted a comparative analysis of various loss functions, including cross-entropy, hinge, and squared error loss functions, by training a model on the MNIST dataset. Our findings indicate that the choice of loss function significantly influences the performance of a classification model.

This paper investigates the stabilization of incompressible fluids governed by the Navier-Stokes equations through boundary feedback controllers in a three-dimensional domain with a flat boundary. We demonstrate that a linear controller, applied to a portion of the boundary and oriented at an angle, can achieve asymptotic stability for any angle between zero and ninety degrees. Our proof relies on establishing a uniform spectral gap for the linearized system's generator, which in turn yields exponential stability.

This research presents a novel numerical simulation that calculates the
thermomechanical behavior of strain-induced crystallization in rubber materials.
The simulation incorporates a cohesive zone model to represent the formation
of cracks and utilizes a regularized phase-field approach to accurately capture
the cracks' evolution. By employing a fully coupled formulation, the simulation
simultaneously accounts for the mechanical and thermal aspects of the problem,
including the heat generated by the mechanical deformation. The proposed
numerical method employs a staggered solution scheme, where the mechanical
equilibrium is solved using a Newton iteration, and the temperature is updated
using a fixed-point iteration. The results demonstrate the model's ability to
accurately capture the strain-induced crack formation and subsequent crack
propagation, as well as the heat distribution within the material. The research
also provides insights into the influence of mechanical loading and temperature
on the crack evolution and the material's overall behavior.

We've calculated the magnetic susceptibility of a three-component triplet Cooper pair in a nematic superconductor using a microscopic approach at temperatures above the critical temperature. Our findings indicate that the magnetic susceptibility can be divided into two parts: the first, arising from the free motion of particles, cannot be described by the simple, non-interacting Boltzmann equation, while the second, influenced by scattering, can. Our calculations also show that the magnetic susceptibility can be broken down into three contributions: the first, related to the density of states, is non-zero for all types of triplet pairing, while the second and third, related to the superfluid velocity, can cancel out the first contribution, potentially leading to a negative total magnetic susceptibility.

In online learning scenarios, a learner can be influenced by two types of feedback: information about the outcome of their actions and guidance on how to improve their performance. In this study, we examine a situation where the feedback provided is non-compliant but can be transformed into useful, optimal information. We develop a novel algorithm that enables the learner to convert a single, rectified response into an ideal, optimal piece of information. This breakthrough has significant implications for various applications, including human-robot interaction, where a robot can be trained to convert a single, unclear signal into a precise, optimal action.

A conventional differential detection method for continuous phase modulation (CPM) is used to eliminate the need for coherent detection, which requires a precise carrier phase and frequency recovery.  However, this method introduces a delay of at least two CPM symbols.  In this paper, we demonstrate that differential detection can be performed with a one-symbol delay for a class of CPM signals, including M-ary CPM with binary data.  We derive the corresponding non-coherent differential detection metric and develop a simplified decision rule.  A simplified metric is also proposed for general CPM signals.  The proposed method's performance is compared to conventional methods through simulations.

The detection of merging neutron stars and black holes by next-generation gravitational wave detectors will enable researchers to investigate the unique case of a neutron star being swallowed by a black hole. This research explores the connection between the properties of the neutron star and the dynamics of the black hole's event horizon, which may produce observable electromagnetic radiation. We examine the impact of core-collapse dynamics on the amount of matter expelled from the system and the resulting electromagnetic signals. Our findings reveal that the mass of the neutron star and the amount of matter expelled are closely related, and that core-collapse dynamics can significantly affect the amount of matter expelled from the system. These results have important implications for the detection of these events using electromagnetic radiation, and can be used to constrain the properties of the neutron star.

We derived an expression for the compressibility gap that is applicable to any system, and we have computed this value for two cases: a scalar field in Minkowski spacetime and a massless Dirac field. We have also established a connection between compressibility and entanglement spectrum, and we have calculated the compressibility gap for the thermal state of the harmonic oscillator. We have also demonstrated that the compressibility gap is related to the entanglement spectrum, and we have found that the quantum compressibility gap for a scalar field in Minkowski spacetime is equal to $k_B T$, and the compressibility itself is infinite. We have also demonstrated that the compressibility gap for a massless Dirac field in Minkowski spacetime is equal to $2.58 k_B T$, and the compressibility itself is infinite. Current techniques for generating rain in clear images rely on artificial rain creation models, which are evaluated using artificially generated rain. In contrast, real rain removal models are assessed using images with natural rain. This evaluation disparity hampers a fair comparison between artificial rain creation and real rain removal models. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that simultaneously achieves artificial rain creation and real rain removal, using a disentangled image translation framework. Our method utilizes two disentangled latent spaces to capture the rain component and the clear background, enabling a unified model to create rain from clear images and remove rain from rainy images. Our method's results demonstrate its ability to produce high-quality rain and accurately remove rain from images, outperforming existing methods in terms of both visual and quantitative metrics.

A popular method for learning reward functions in reinforcement learning is through preference-based learning, where a human provides feedback in the form of pairwise comparisons. However, this approach can be time-consuming due to the large number of comparisons needed to gather sufficient data. In this paper, we propose a more efficient approach by grouping trajectories into clusters and having a human rank the clusters instead. We develop a novel algorithm that can learn rewards from these ranked clusters, and demonstrate through experiments that our method achieves comparable performance to preference-based learning with significantly fewer human interactions.

The continuum problem's resolution relies on a model that satisfies a specific partnership model with another model that has a definable continuum. This paper examines the impact of various models on potential solutions, including those with a Suslin tree, a Jensen tree, a Kurepa tree, and multiple square principles. The discussion of model partnerships is expanded to include additional models such as HOD, PFA, and NS, and the concept of a definable continuum is explored in greater depth.

This study examines the integral equation associated with the Q-curvature type equation on a bounded domain in R^n, and proves that the equation has a positive solution under specific conditions, which can be achieved through the method of Q-operators.

This study examines the relationship between the Five Factor Model of personality and drug consumption risk, focusing on the assessment of drug consumption risk through personality evaluation. Researchers collected data from 1,000 participants aged 18 to 65, who completed the NEO-PI-R personality test and a drug consumption risk assessment. The results revealed a significant correlation between the Five Factor Model and drug consumption risk, with neuroticism and conscientiousness being the most influential factors. The study found that personality evaluation can effectively assess drug consumption risk, with implications for the development of prevention and intervention programs.

We introduce ATOMIC, an open-source framework comprising an atlas of machine intelligence and an If-Then reasoning engine. ATOMIC integrates a vast array of existing AI tools and models into a unified interface, enabling the creation of sophisticated problem-solving systems. By leveraging the modular nature of machine intelligence, we can combine the strengths of various AI components to address complex tasks that exceed the capabilities of individual models. We showcase the effectiveness of If-Then reasoning by developing an intelligent system that can summarize lengthy scientific articles, outperforming both standalone AI models and human writers in terms of coherence and comprehensibility. We also explore the potential of If-Then reasoning in other domains, such as legal argumentation and news summarization, highlighting the versatility and scalability of this approach.

This study presents NISQ-HHL, a portfolio optimization method that leverages the HHL algorithm for solving sparse, well-conditioned linear systems. By utilizing this algorithm, we can reduce the number of circuit depth iterations and achieve a logarithmic complexity in terms of precision. We have implemented NISQ-HHL on actual hardware using the IBM Quantum Experience, specifically on the IBM Quantum Experience's 5-qubit and 16-qubit processors. The results indicate that NISQ-HHL outperforms other quantum and classical optimization methods in terms of solution quality and runtime.

This paper presents a novel approach to training BERT-based models for speech recognition using a multi-modal learning method. By combining text and audio data, we employ a bidirectional focus method to train the models. Our experiments show that this approach yields significant improvements in speech recognition accuracy, with a 0.5% reduction in Word Error Rate (WER) when using both audio and text data compared to audio data alone.

In the context of Hadron-Iron collisions at 18 GeV, a detailed examination of the total cross section's time-dependent fluctuations was undertaken. By dividing the data into 10-nanosecond intervals, a fluctuation parameter was calculated and its connection to the average cross section's behavior was established. A notable inverse relationship was found, where lower average cross section values correspond to a higher fluctuation parameter. To investigate the underlying causes, a Monte Carlo simulation was conducted, which confirmed the observed relationship. A distinct pattern was identified in the data, where a specific range of average cross section values exhibited a consistent fluctuation parameter value. This finding was further explored by calculating the cross correlation between adjacent data points, which indicated a memory effect within the system.

This study examines the average first entry value of random parking functions generated according to the Dukes-Horv\'ath model, specifically focusing on positions $k$ that grow at a rate of $n^\alpha$, where $0<\alpha<1$. 

Our findings reveal that, as the length of the function $n$ increases, the distribution of values at these designated positions converges to a distinct limiting distribution determined by $\alpha$. 

Additionally, we derive analogous results for a related model of random parking functions, where the distribution of values at positions $k$ growing as $n^\alpha$ in the B\'erczi-Horv\'ath model also exhibits convergent behavior with similar asymptotic properties.

Researchers have long been investigating the unique electrical properties of superconducting nanowires, particularly their ability to conduct electricity in a coherent state. In this study, we examined the behavior of lead-based nanowires with varying widths and found that their electrical properties can be controlled by applying a gate voltage. We observed that the conductance of the nanowires can be modulated between zero and discrete quantum units, and that this behavior is influenced by the width of the nanowires. Our analysis suggests that the conductance of narrow wires is controlled by quantum phase slips, while wider wires exhibit a Coulomb blockade effect. These findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of superconducting nanowires and may have implications for the development of quantum computing technologies.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 was a significant milestone in astronomy, achieved by identifying the first known T-dwarf through a serendipitous observation. Since then, GJ 229B has been extensively studied, with various spectroscopic observations conducted to analyze its atmospheric composition. Despite these efforts, the abundance of alkali metals on GJ 229B has remained enigmatic, with conflicting results obtained from different analysis methods. In this study, we utilized the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze high-resolution near-infrared spectra of GJ 229B, with the goal of resolving the long-standing mystery of its alkali metal abundances. Our findings indicate that the metal abundances of Na and K on GJ 229B are elevated by approximately 1 dex, with the best-fitting models suggesting that the metal abundances are 1.5 and 1.2 dex higher than solar levels, respectively. Our results also suggest that the atmospheric temperature of GJ 229B is likely between 600 and 700 K, with the metal abundances of Na and K being consistent with the elevated metal content found in the white dwarf system of HD 41004.

Lattice QCD calculations have been used to model the properties of the quark-gluon plasma, 
and a study has been conducted to determine the structure functions of virtual deep inelastic scattering 
on this fluid. The calculations are based on the quark propagators derived from the background fields 
of the quark-gluon plasma, and the results show that the structure functions of virtual deep inelastic 
scattering can be accurately predicted using a pQCD approach. The results also indicate that the 
structure functions of virtual DIS can be used to determine the properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

This paper introduces a novel approach to New View Video Prediction (NVVP), 
which leverages a dual representation of 3D shapes and optical flow to generate
high-quality output frames. By combining these two representations, our method
achieves superior results in terms of both visual appearance and motion consistency.
Our approach involves using a shape representation network to extract shape features,
which are then used to predict optical flow and generate the output frame.
Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, which outperforms
state-of-the-art NVVP techniques in terms of both PSNR and SSIM metrics.

In the context of quantum mechanics, adjacent energy levels within a system can interact through a process known as inter-level coupling, which is an essential component of various applications, including quantum information processing and the study of chaotic systems. This phenomenon is typically examined using a two-level system within each energy state. Our research utilizes a quantum dot coupled to a single-mode cavity to demonstrate the significance of inter-level coupling in a three-level system. By analyzing the system's dynamics through time-resolved measurements, we found that the interaction between the dot and the cavity enables the transfer of a quantum state from one basis state to another, bypassing intermediate states. This capability can be harnessed to develop more efficient quantum algorithms and explore the behavior of complex, chaotic systems.

The $\Omega^{-}$ baryon, which contains three strange quarks, is a crucial component of LHCb's Strange Hadron Programme. Its resonance states, which have not yet been observed, can be studied using proton-proton collision data at the LHC. By applying a likelihood fit to the $K^-K^-\pi^+$ mass spectrum in $p\bar{p}$ collision data, we have identified the $\Omega^{-}$ and its excited states. Our findings yield a mass of 1672.45 GeV/c$^2$ and a width of 8.23 GeV/c$^2$ for the $\Omega^{-}$, which are in good agreement with previous measurements and theoretical predictions.

This study examines the utility of a uniform mixing model in forecasting disease transmission among passengers on an urban bus, specifically in Tokyo. We analyze the spread of infectious diseases by applying a basic Susceptible-Infectious model and compare its predictions to those of a model that accounts for individual interactions. Utilizing a real-world dataset of passenger counts on the Tokyo Metro, we find that models based on uniform mixing accurately reflect observed transmission rates, with only minor discrepancies observed. These findings suggest that uniform mixing models can effectively forecast disease transmission in confined urban spaces, offering a practical and efficient approach to public health planning.

Quantum electrodynamics predicts that the vacuum behaves like a birefringent material due to interactions between virtual particles, an effect that can be amplified by applying strong external fields.  This phenomenon, known as vacuum birefringence, is expected to be observable in astrophysical settings, such as near magnetars, where extremely strong magnetic fields are present.  However, detecting this effect is challenging due to the weak birefringence caused by the EFT and the difficulty in distinguishing its impact from other sources of polarization in X-ray emissions.  To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed using a correlation-based detection method that can filter out unrelated polarization fluctuations and focus on the birefringence effect.  This method has been shown to be effective in detecting the EFT-induced birefringence in laboratory settings, and may also be applicable to observations of magnetars.  Additionally, researchers have explored the possibility of detecting the vacuum diffraction effect, which is another prediction of QED, by analyzing the polarization of X-ray emissions from magnetars.  Although the diffraction effect is even more difficult to detect than birefringence, it may be possible to observe its impact on the polarization of X-rays as they pass through the electron diffraction pattern in the accretion disk of a magnetar.

This note outlines the methodology employed by J. A. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to identify fully transitive polyhedra, employing a streamlined approach to verify the convex hull of a group action. This method is subsequently applied to classify the action of $M_{11}$ on 65 points, resulting in a polyhedron with 11 faces and 66 vertices.

We revisit the uncloneable encryption concept originally proposed by Alwen, Azar, and Pietrzak in 2013, addressing an issue with their primary construction and presenting an alternative approach. Our new method achieves a more efficient solution, utilizing a shorter encryption key and shorter cloned ciphertexts compared to their previous method. Specifically, our construction relies on a simpler assumption, namely Learning With Rounding, and offers the following advantages: a shorter key and cloned ciphertext of nearly the same size as the underlying LRN instance, and a straightforward reduction that requires just one cloning query.

This study explores keyless verification techniques for secure communication in noisy environments, where a transmitter and receiver generate a shared secret through interaction with a random signal, and confirm their knowledge of this secret without the need for pre-shared keys. We analyze two methods for confirming their shared knowledge: one where the receiver initiates the process and another where the transmitter does so. We derive optimal strategies for both parties to maximize the minimum security of the process, and identify conditions under which secure communication is possible. We also investigate the performance of these techniques in real-world scenarios and compare them to existing methods.
