In late 2019 Forsage, a multi-level marketing scheme disguised as a cryptocurrency venture, defrauded its investors of approximately $360 million before being shut down by the Ethereum community. Forsage's downfall was hastened by a whistleblower who exposed the scheme's inner workings on social media, prompting a detailed analysis of its structure and the role of open-source code in its collapse. This study delves into the specifics of Forsage's operation, providing a comprehensive examination of its code and the motivations behind the actions of its participants.

We have identified 19 new globular clusters in the Milky Way's bulge region, bringing the total number of known clusters in this area to 59. These newly discovered clusters were found using the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) survey, which covers a wide area of the Milky Way's bulge. To confirm their authenticity, we used photometric methods to analyze color-magnitude diagrams and determine that each candidate has a distinct concentration of stars at the tip of the red giant branch. Additionally, we used the VVUFS variable star catalogue to rule out any confusion with other celestial objects. For each cluster, we estimated their distances, ages, and metallicities, and found that they span a wide range of metallicities from -1.0 to +0.2. We also found that the newly discovered clusters have a wide range of distances from the galactic center, and that they are distributed across the Milky Way's bulge region.

Our study examines the theoretical framework for Drell-Yan production in a scenario where a massive quark from the proton interacts with a gluon, and we derive an analytical formula for the cross-section at next-to-leading order in the quark mass. Additionally, we explore the impact of including a soft cutoff on the quark's mass, which is necessary for accurately describing experimental data. We also investigate the validity of perturbative calculations at lower energy scales and find that non-perturbative effects become significant when the quark's mass is comparable to the dilepton mass. To address this, we introduce a method to combine the perturbative calculation with non-singular contributions from the parton distribution function, enabling a more precise comparison with experimental data. Our analysis of existing Drell-Yan data suggests that including this effect can improve the fit and may provide insights into the structure of the proton at low energy scales.

The accuracy of tight-binding models used in condensed matter physics is heavily influenced by the choice of basis functions, and recent research has shown that these models can be applied to photonic crystals and other systems when the functions are treated as complex-valued. This study investigates the general properties of such tight-binding models in relation to light-matter interactions, and it is demonstrated that the model's behavior remains consistent regardless of the method used to generate the basis functions, as long as they are orthogonal. Additionally, it is found that the model's invariance to certain transformations can be used to derive a sum rule for the optical conductivity, and this result is applied to investigate the conductivity of graphene and a photonic crystal.

We have developed a new type of holographic error correction code, called hyper-invariant MERA (hMERA), which is suitable for representing systems with power-law correlations. This code is inspired by the invariant MERA (iMERA) that was previously used to model critical systems, and it is based on a different type of tensor network structure. Like iMERA, hMERA is capable of correcting errors, and it can recover from errors that affect a significant portion of the system. This property is similar to that of the holographic error correction code based on AdS/CFT, and it is also related to the concept of homological maximally recoverable quantum codes. We have demonstrated that hMERA can be used to correct errors that affect up to a significant fraction of the system, and it can recover from errors that affect the entire system. This property is similar to that of the holographic error correction code based on AdS/CFT, and it is also related to the concept of homological maximally recoverable quantum codes. We have also shown that hMERA can be used to correct errors that affect up to a significant fraction of the system, and it can recover from errors that affect the entire system. This property is similar to that of the holographic error correction code based on AdS/CFT, and it is also related to the concept of homological maximally recoverable quantum codes.

A computational study of retinal's photoisomerization from all-trans to 11-cis form was conducted using a semi-empirical tight-binding tight-binding Hamiltonian and a nonadiabatic Lindblad master equation. The study found that retinal's reactivity increases significantly with rising temperature, particularly at higher temperatures, and that reactivity varies greatly depending on the specific vibrational mode that is excited, with some modes leading to much faster isomerization rates than others.

This paper examines various deep learning models, including LSTM, GRU, and
Feed-Forward Neural Networks, to assess their effectiveness in understanding and
forecasting business processes. We develop a new dataset to represent process
events and their associated attributes, then apply multiple deep learning models to
this data. Our analysis reveals that the LSTM model outperforms other models in
predicting business processes, achieving a 90% accuracy rate.

This study examines Twitter data to gauge public response during and after the Izmir earthquake that struck on October 30, 2020. By analyzing 1.1 million tweets, we identified key topics and emotions expressed by users. Our findings reveal that topics related to the earthquake and rescue efforts were most prevalent, while emotions of fear and sadness were most common. Furthermore, we found that users' activity levels peaked in the hours following the event and declined in the days that followed.

We establish that specific types of functions within the space $C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^d)$, which have Schwartz-type characteristics in both time and frequency domains, cannot vanish over an entire subspace of a certain dimension, and we demonstrate the non-zero nature of certain Toeplitz operators acting on this space.

The 1985 AD Leo X-ray flare was the most intense stellar flare ever recorded, with a duration of over 10 hours and a peak brightness 1000 times greater than any other known X-ray flare.  This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the near-ultraviolet continuum spectrum of the AD Leo during the peak of the 1985 flare, using archival data from the IUE satellite.  The study reveals that the continuum spectrum of the AD Leo during the peak of the flare was dominated by hydrogen recombination, with a high electron temperature of 100,000 K and a high electron density of 10^12 cm^-3.  The study also reveals that the hydrogen Lyman-alpha line was significantly broadened, with a full width at half maximum of 1.5 Angstroms, and that the hydrogen Lyman-beta line was also significantly enhanced, with a flux of 10^-12 erg cm^-2 s^-1.  The study suggests that the high electron temperature and density observed during the peak of the flare were likely caused by a powerful magnetic reconnection event, which released a massive amount of energy and heated the surrounding plasma to extremely high temperatures.  The study also suggests that the high electron density observed during the peak of the flare was likely caused by a powerful shock wave, which compressed the surrounding plasma and increased its density significantly.  The study concludes that the high electron temperature

In this study, we examine the PT-symmetric property within a periodic waveguide system that includes multiple PT-symmetric unit cells. We analyze how waves move through this system and find that certain conditions can be met to achieve CPAL in specific cells while maintaining transparency in the rest of the system. We also explore the effects of PT-symmetric symmetry breaking on wave transmission and find that it can lead to a sharp increase in the coherent lasing component. We derive a condition for the PT-symmetric system to exhibit complete transparency and find that it can be met with various combinations of coupling strengths. We further investigate how breaking the PT-symmetric symmetry affects wave transmission and find that it can lead to a coherent perfect lasing component that can be controlled by adjusting the breaking strength. We also derive an expression for the transmission coefficient that can be used to understand the interplay between the coherent transparency and lasing components. Our findings provide a pathway for the design of PT-symmetric devices that can exhibit CPAL and controlled lasing.

Complex Boolean networks under study exhibit dynamic behavior that can be categorized into two primary patterns: stable equilibrium states and intricate dynamics characterized by activity fluctuations. This dichotomy is influenced by the interplay between system parameters and interaction strengths, which can be visualized through a phase diagram. Our investigation reveals that an additional factor, namely the sparsity level, significantly impacts this dynamic landscape. As the system's sparsity increases, distinct transitions occur, shifting the system from static equilibrium to dynamic fluctuations and ultimately to chaotic behavior. Notably, these transitions are accompanied by abrupt changes in system activity, which exhibit characteristics reminiscent of those observed in activity fluctuating systems. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of the dynamic behavior of sparse Boolean systems and highlights the critical role of sparsity in shaping system activity fluctuations.

This study derives explicit analytical formulas for calculating the matrix elements of any one-body and two-body operators between any two Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions. These types of independent particle basis states are extensively utilized in nuclear mean field theories.

3D point cloud models are frequently distorted by noise and incomplete data,
which can be addressed by point cloud completion techniques.
However, conventional completion methods often yield inconsistent results due
to the ambiguity caused by multiple possible surface solutions.
To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel framework called TPC, which uniquely
resolves surface solutions by applying a dual strategy of data-driven learning
and geometrically-informed regularization.
TPC achieves this through a two-pronged approach, combining a unique
regularization loss function with a robust point cloud completion network.
The network is trained to learn a mapping from a transformed point cloud to its
corresponding completed surface, which is then used to uniquely resolve the
surface ambiguity.
TPC is evaluated on two widely-used benchmarks, ShapeNet and ModelNet, and
demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

This paper investigates the application of medium access control techniques, specifically ALOHA and CSMA, in radar networks utilizing FMCW technology. We examine various transmission methods, including slotted ALOHA, ALOHA, time division multiple access, and multiple access with collision avoidance, to assess their effectiveness in reducing interference and enhancing network performance. We develop a mathematical model to analyze the network's throughput and interference levels, and we validate our findings through simulations. Our results indicate that ALOHA and CSMA methods can be effective in radar networks, and that the optimal method depends on the network's size and traffic patterns.

This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal knowledge graph completion, 
utilizing a dual-component representation model that combines low-rank embeddings 
with a model-agnostic component. Our method effectively captures both the 
inherent properties of triples in the temporal knowledge graph and their dynamic 
evolution over time. To enhance prediction accuracy, we employ a contrastive 
learning strategy that leverages temporal information to refine the graph's 
temporal representations. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various 
temporal knowledge graph prediction tasks, including link prediction, fact 
prediction, and multi-task prediction. Our model achieves state-of-the-art 
performance on three widely used benchmark datasets. To further investigate the 
underlying mechanisms of temporal knowledge graphs, we conduct extensive 
experiments and visual analyses to examine the low-rank embeddings, the 
contrastive loss, and the impact of different hyperparameters.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function has been utilized to determine the intricate eigenenergy of the vibrational energy distribution in $^{16}$O, but a specific RPA pole strength is required for this calculation. This study proposes a new approach to calculate this eigenenergy by considering the interplay between RPA excitations and non-interacting single-particle excitations. This new approach yields more precise results for properties like energy and density, and when applied to $^{16}$O, it reveals that the intricate ground state energy within the RPA framework is 20.3 MeV higher than the exact ground state energy. This discrepancy is primarily due to the RPA framework's failure to account for the intricate correlations in the ground state, specifically the coupling between RPA excitations and single-particle excitations.

This research proposes an innovative method for grouping complex systems, such as those found in physics, using data-driven techniques. The underlying principle is that systems with similar long-term behavior patterns can be classified into distinct categories. To achieve this, a cutting-edge algorithm called ResNet is utilized to analyze the dynamics of the systems in question. The results demonstrate that this method can effectively identify multiple coexisting stable states, or attractors, in a variety of physical systems, including the Lorenz system, a system with multiple basins of periodic behavior, and a system with chaotic dynamics.

Text generation models based on Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have
achieved remarkable results, but current models based on N-gram GANs suffer from
limited vocabulary size and poor model interpretability. To address these
shortcomings, we propose a novel model called SparseGAN, which utilizes sparse
vectors to represent words and employs a sparse variational autoencoder to
generate words. By doing so, SparseGAN not only expands the vocabulary size but
also enhances the interpretability of the model. Experimental results on two
text generation datasets demonstrate that SparseGAN outperforms traditional
N-gram models in terms of perplexity and human evaluation.

The concept of interstellar pansomia, which involves the transfer of life between galaxies through space, is a fascinating yet controversial topic that has captivated the human imagination. This study explores the possibility of interstellar pansomia by analyzing the transfer of terrestrial life from Earth to Mars via meteorites. The study focuses on the survival of life within meteorites during their journey through space and the conditions required for life to remain viable. The study finds that while some life forms can survive in meteorites for extended periods, the conditions required for life to remain viable are extremely rare and unlikely to occur frequently. The study also discusses the implications of interstellar pansomia on the search for extraterrestrial life and the need for further research to better understand the conditions required for life to transfer between planets.

We utilize a disturbance-based theoretical framework to forecast the interference patterns between foreground and mapping signals in intensity mapping experiments. Our predictions are corroborated by simulations, which also allow us to assess the impact of foreground cleaning techniques on the data. Our findings reveal that the interference patterns are significantly influenced by the characteristics of the mapping data, particularly its spatial distribution, and that the interference patterns can be mitigated through foreground removal techniques. Our predictions are applicable to a range of mapping experiments, including those conducted with the Square Kilometre Array and the PUMA telescope.

We have discovered a novel phenomenon in certain systems with U(N) symmetry, where the symmetry is disrupted spontaneously, leading to the creation of smaller subgroups with progressively reduced symmetries. This phenomenon occurs in a chain-like manner, where the disruption of one symmetry leads to the creation of the next, smaller subgroup. We have derived a general formula for the length of this chain, which is determined by the initial group size N. We have also demonstrated that this phenomenon can be observed in a quantum Ising model, which exhibits an infinite chain of symmetry disruptions when the initial group is U(∞). We have also investigated the relationship between this phenomenon and the concept of large N, which is commonly used in quantum field theory.

A significant aspect of modern population studies is understanding how populations interact with various resources. This study expands spatial capture-recapture models to integrate data on resource usage from marked individuals, thereby enhancing our ability to estimate population size and density while considering their relationship with different resources. We developed a new methodology that leverages information on resource utilization from captured animals to estimate population parameters and explore the connection between animals and their resources. Our approach was tested using simulated data and real-world data from a study on giant pandas in China. The results showed that our method can accurately estimate population size and density, as well as identify areas of high animal utilization. By incorporating resource utilization data into capture-recapture models, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of population dynamics and their relationship with the environment.
We present an approximation algorithm for finding minimum power $k$ edge distinct $st$-paths in a graph, achieving O($\sqrt{k}$) power, with a running time of O($k^2$) times that of minimum $st$-cut.

This study proposes a decentralized approach for managing unmanned aerial vehicle swarms in dynamic environments. The approach enables each UAV to independently assess its surroundings and adjust its position to achieve optimal swarm positioning without relying on external positioning systems. By utilizing onboard sensors and communication systems, the approach allows the swarms to adapt to changing environmental conditions and avoid obstacles. The approach is validated through simulations and real-world tests, demonstrating its effectiveness in maneuvering swarms through narrow passages and around obstacles.

Local interactions within complex systems often lead to dynamic processes that exhibit localized behavior, which can be observed in various contexts, including brain activity, fire spread, and epidemic transmission. A key indicator of this localized behavior is the slowing down of a process as a control parameter is adjusted, which can be quantified using the concept of dynamic criticality. This phenomenon has been extensively studied in the context of percolation theory, where the critical point is associated with the onset of a process. However, many processes occur within interconnected networks, which can significantly impact their dynamics. In this study, we investigate the relationship between dynamic criticality and graph topology in a broad range of one-dimensional processes on different types of networks. Our findings reveal that the critical point is not solely determined by the network's structure, but rather by the interplay between the process and the network. We also identify specific network features that promote or hinder localized behavior, which can provide valuable insights for understanding and manipulating dynamic processes in complex networks.

This research focuses on assessing the effectiveness of players' defensive positions in the UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022 tournaments, employing a statistical approach called Generalized Valuation of Defense (GVD). By estimating the likelihood of a player being in a specific location, GVD allows for a comparison of the spatial distribution of players across different matches. The results indicate that the location of players in the UEFA EURO 2020 and 2022 tournaments was not entirely optimal, with some teams demonstrating more efficient defensive positioning than others. The study also highlights the importance of considering the movement of players in real-time, as well as the need for further research to develop more effective strategies for positioning players in defensive roles.

Extracting information from images of documents is a crucial task in many industries, and it's often complicated by the vast differences in document layouts. Although there are successful methods for processing specific document types, they rely on pre-defined templates that match the document's structure. In this study, we explore a more versatile approach that doesn't require templates and can handle a wide range of document formats. Our method uses a novel, multi-task learning approach that combines two key components: a visual attention mechanism that identifies important areas of the image, and a position-aware decoder that extracts information from those areas. Our approach is trained using only the content of the documents, and we've achieved impressive results on two challenging datasets, outperforming previous methods that used templates and human-annotated bounding boxes.

This study introduces a novel approach to recurrent state space models that can handle dynamic systems with unknown parameters. The proposed method, called Hidden Parameter RSSM (HP-RSSM), automatically incorporates new data points into the model's internal representation of its state and parameters, eliminating the need for a separate model update step. The HP-RSSM model is built upon the Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2015) factor analysis framework and is evaluated through various experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets. The results indicate that HP-RSSM outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of predictive accuracy and model adaptability.

This study reveals that the type $B$ freeness of a set of random matrices remains stable under small, random changes in the matrices. Building on this finding, we apply it to derive the conditional free distribution of $n \times n$ random matrices, given their size, as the size approaches infinity.

We examine genus 3 maps from genus 1 curves and analyze their Prym varieties, which are genus 2 curves. We demonstrate that these curves' isomorphism class can be derived from the genus 2 curve's isomorphism class and further, we establish a genus 1 curve's isomorphism class from the genus 2 curve's isomorphism class, a genus 2 map from the genus 1 curve, and specific numerical data. We also explore genus 3 maps from genus 1 curves that yield genus 2 curves isomorphic to each other, and provide a method to recover the genus 1 curve's isomorphism class from the genus 2 curve's isomorphism class, the genus 2 map, and numerical data.

Structural polarization in complex networks is a significant characteristic that distinguishes them from one another. However, the influence of network degree distribution on structural polarization complicates its interpretation. To address this issue, we have developed a new metric, the normalized polarization coefficient, to systematically evaluate the structural polarization of networks. By analyzing various types of polarized networks, we found that our coefficient can accurately capture the relationship between structural polarization and degree distribution. Furthermore, we discovered that the normalized polarization coefficient can be used to quantitatively predict the structure of networks based on their polarization levels. To further validate our findings, we applied the coefficient to real-world networks and obtained consistent results.

The behavior of multilayer networks is influenced by the interplay between their separate layers and interconnections. This paper examines how multiple layers of oscillators, which follow the Curie-Weiss model, affect the transmission of synchronization solutions across layers. We analyze how changes in interlayer coupling impact the multilayer system's ability to transmit solutions and identify conditions under which certain solutions become unstable. Notably, we find that solutions with higher levels of desynchronization in one layer can lead to increased levels of synchronization in another layer.

The stress operator $\mathbb{C}: \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}\to \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ is linear and characterizes the mechanical properties of a material. Its decomposition into an isotropic component and a deviatoric operator $\mathbb{D}$, where $\mathbb{D}$ is invariant under rotation, is explored. The article demonstrates that the minimum parameterization of $\mathbb{C}$ necessitates nine parameters, consisting of three parameters for the isotropic component and six parameters for $\mathbb{D}$. Additionally, the article investigates the geometric properties of the image of the deviatoric operator under the set of deviatoric matrices.

Effective program testing is crucial for identifying bugs and ensuring the reliability of software systems. This paper introduces a novel approach to testing that leverages geometry and topology concepts to explore the testing space and pinpoint areas requiring additional test cases. By employing a geometric method, we can visualize the testing process and pinpoint areas of the program that have not been sufficiently tested. Our approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a program for calculating the area of a triangle, and we discuss its potential applications and future directions.

We introduce HyperPrompt, a novel architecture that leverages hypernetworks to
create task-specific prompt representations, which condition transformer models
on particular tasks. HyperPrompt can be seamlessly integrated with various transformer
models, such as BERT, GPT-2, and T5, and can be easily adapted to multiple tasks by
fine-tuning the hypernetwork. Experiments conducted on the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks
demonstrate the effectiveness of HyperPrompt, resulting in substantial performance
improvements over baseline models and significant reductions in training time.
Furthermore, HyperPrompt outperforms alternative task-conditioning methods,
including cross-task attention mechanisms and task-specific hypernetwork-driven
prompt representations.

This paper continues the exploration of a specific phenomenon in various mathematical objects, where a set of vectors in a given object can be arranged in a way that the sum of any $n$ vectors positioned on the boundary of a given shape equals zero. This property is examined in detail for Weyl chambers of type $C_n$, root systems of type $D_n$, and the positive roots of type $B_n$.

We have developed a novel concept for protecting the parity symmetry of a system, 
resulting in a unique phenomenon - package emission. This occurs when a parity-protected 
system undergoes a transition to a lower-energy state, releasing a photon and transitioning 
to an empty state. The concept of parity protection is based on a system consisting of two 
identical sub-systems, where the parity symmetry is maintained by the exchange of the sub-systems. 
This symmetry is used to create a package emission process, where the system emits a photon 
and transitions to an empty state. 
The concept of parity protection is applied to a system consisting of two identical two-level 
atoms, where the parity symmetry is maintained by the exchange of the atoms. 
This symmetry is used to create a package emission process, where the system emits a photon 
and transitions to an empty state. 
The concept of parity protection is also applied to a system consisting of two identical 
quantum dots, where the parity symmetry is maintained by the exchange of the quantum dots. 
This symmetry is used to create a package emission process, where the system emits a photon 
and transitions to an empty state. 
The concept of parity protection is also applied to a system consisting of two identical 
superconducting qubits, where the parity symmetry is maintained by the exchange of the qubits. 
This symmetry is used to create a package emission process, where the system emits a photon 
and transitions to an empty state.

This paper introduces a new network scale estimation algorithm that operates effectively in a small-world network environment, taking into account the malicious actions of a limited number of participants. The proposed method is implemented within a probabilistic framework, where the scale is determined by the network's diameter, and the algorithm's efficiency is influenced by the number of malicious participants. The network scale estimation is achieved with a time complexity of O(n^2) and a space complexity of O(n), and the algorithm's performance is verified through a series of simulations.

Evaluating road network performance and optimizing traffic management require
accurate traffic data.  This study focuses on estimating short-term queue lengths
at signalized intersections without assuming a specific traffic model.  By using
data from probe vehicles, we develop a nonparametric estimation method based on
the first and last points of the queue.  We propose a novel approach to identify
these queue points, which we validate through extensive simulations and real-world
data.  Our results show that our method can accurately estimate queue lengths,
with a mean absolute error of 4.4 vehicles, and outperform existing methods.

In numerical general relativity, solving the initial data constraints using a traditional method can be challenging due to the non-linearity and elliptic nature of the equations. A new method has been developed to address this issue by applying a conformal transformation to the metric and extrinsic curvature, which linearizes the Hamiltonian constraint and simplifies the momentum constraints into an algebraic problem. This approach, known as CTTK, allows for a more efficient solution to the initial data constraints by solving the momentum constraints algebraically and then using a standard multigrid solver to solve the Hamiltonian constraint. A key advantage of CTTK is that it can handle binary black hole spacetimes with high accuracy and can be used to generate initial data for binary black hole mergers with high precision. A comparison with other methods shows that CTTK is a more accurate and computationally efficient method for solving the initial data constraints in numerical relativity.

The LHCb collaboration has analyzed $\Sigma^+ \to p \ell^+ \ell^-$ decays, where the LHCb data includes 3.8 inverse femtobarns of $pp$ collision data at 7 and 8 TeV. By focusing on the dimuon mode, the research establishes the first evidence for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay, with a significance of 4.2 standard deviations. Additionally, constraints on branching fractions for both dimuon and mixed lepton modes are determined, with the dimuon mode having a branching fraction of $(4.9^{+2.1}_{-1.9}) \times 10^{-10}$ and the mixed lepton mode having a combined upper limit of $1.1 \times 10^{-9}$ at a 90% confidence level.

The Nernst effect, which involves generating a transverse electric field in response to a temperature gradient under a magnetic field, is a well-known phenomenon in condensed matter physics.  However, an unusual type of Nernst effect, which can also be induced by a magnetic field perpendicular to the temperature gradient, is being investigated in this study.  Researchers are exploring this effect in epitaxial Mn$_3$NiN thin films, which exhibit strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and can be manipulated into different magnetic states through the application of a gate voltage.  By measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient in these films, the study reveals that the effect is significantly stronger in the antiferromagnetic state compared to the ferromagnetic state, a finding that is attributed to the unique properties of the material's magnetic structure.  The study also investigates the impact of disorder on the unusual Nernst effect, which is found to be influenced by the material's carrier concentration and mobility.

Labeled data generated by multiple human annotators is frequently used in tasks like object detection and image classification, but it often contains inconsistencies due to varying levels of expertise and subjectivity. To address this issue, researchers have proposed using ensemble methods to generate more accurate and reliable labels, but traditional approaches have limitations when dealing with bounding box data due to the high computational cost of non-linear aggregation methods. In response, we introduce an innovative approach called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), which utilizes multi-instructor knowledge distillation to automatically generate high-quality labels from multiple annotators. PILE leverages soft labels generated by each instructor and refines them through an iterative process, resulting in improved label quality and performance. Our approach has been shown to outperform existing methods on the Visual Object Detection Quality (VIDO) dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating accurate and reliable labels for object detection tasks.

This lecture will provide an overview of beam dynamics and reductions in circular accelerators, focusing on key aspects such as the influence of magnetic fields on particle motion, the dynamics of transverse and longitudinal motion, and the development of beam reductions.

User facilities, such as synchrotron and X-ray free-electron laser research centers, offer exceptional tools for studying various materials and biological samples. To take full advantage of these resources, researchers rely on user interfaces that provide access to these tools. However, the growing number of simultaneous experiments and the associated complexity of operating these tools has made it increasingly difficult for researchers to manage their time effectively. This challenge has been addressed by the development of machine intelligence tools, which have been integrated into the control interfaces of these facilities. These tools automate routine tasks, provide real-time data analysis, and enable researchers to run multiple experiments remotely. As a result, researchers can focus on the scientific aspects of their research, while the machine intelligence tools handle the operational aspects. This approach has been successfully implemented at several user facilities, including the Advanced Photon Source, and is expected to become the standard for future research centers.
This article examines the local regularity of solutions to a time-dependent obstacle issue in the context of parabolic $q$-growth functionals, where $q$ varies between 2 and infinity.

This study revisits the linearized Geodesic Acoustic Mode (GAM) equation for a toroidal plasma, taking into account the anisotropic temperature effects. By applying a local mode analysis, we derive a dispersion relation that incorporates anisotropic temperatures and a magnetic well. Our findings reveal that anisotropic ion temperatures significantly influence GAM frequency, while anisotropic electron temperatures have a negligible effect. Additionally, we explore the impact of anisotropic temperatures on GAM mode saturation and derive a saturated amplitude relation. Our saturated amplitude analysis indicates that anisotropic temperatures can lead to a non-Gaussian saturated GAM density fluctuation amplitude, which aligns with recent experimental observations.

Quantum annealing's effectiveness is hindered by Hamiltonians that are non-stoquastic in nature, as their associated Green's function Monte Carlo simulations encounter exponential growth in computational time due to probability distribution collapse. This exponential increase in 'negative probabilities' is equivalent to the growth of the annealing time, making such Hamiltonians unsuitable for quantum annealing applications. Interestingly, adding a stochastic element to the Hamiltonian results in a quadratic growth of 'negative probabilities', indicating that environmental noise can actually be beneficial in this context.

This study delves into the background of Dutch astronomer Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who served as the director of Kapteyn's Astronomical Laboratory from 1920 to 1940. The research highlights the laboratory's unique position in the Netherlands during that time, which was characterized by a scarcity of professional astronomers. The study also examines the innovative "Selected Areas" scheme implemented by van Rhijn, which was designed to maximize the laboratory's output by assigning research projects to staff and students based on their specific skills and interests. The research further discusses the scheme's underlying principles, which were influenced by the emerging field of systems theory, as well as its limitations and the challenges faced by the laboratory during its operation. The study provides valuable insights into the management and organization of astronomical research during the early 20th century, and sheds light on the significant contributions made by van Rhijn and his team to the field.
This paper offers a Kummer-theoretic proof of the weight-modulo-deep-level surjectivity for clear classical Iwasawa algebras related to GL_2 over p-adic number fields.

We introduce a novel concept, isoperimetric residues, for compact, connected, oriented hypersurfaces in Rn+1 that separate space into two regions. These residues are defined as the difference between the portions of the outer and inner domains where the hypersurface does not partition and the overall mean curvature. We demonstrate that isoperimetric residues are non-negative and provide a precise characterization of points with minimal density, which correspond to points on the boundary of either domain. Furthermore, we establish a connection between small isoperimetric residues and local regularity, specifically, if a hypersurface has constant mean curvature and a bounded isoperimetric residue, it can be approximated by a C1,1 hypersurface.

This paper introduces a novel technique called Regional Critic Training (RCT) to tackle the issue of imbalanced gradient updates in model-parallel learning of deep neural networks. By dividing the network into regions and training separate critics for each section, RCT enables more balanced gradient updates. We have tested our approach on various large-scale image classification tasks using the ResNet-101 architecture with model-parallel learning, and the results show significant improvements in accuracy compared to traditional methods. Specifically, RCT outperforms the standard data-parallel approach and other model-parallel techniques, achieving a 1.5% accuracy boost on the ImageNet dataset.

A new approach to damage detection and characterization in composite materials is proposed, utilizing electrical impedance tomography (EIT) and genetic algorithms. Unlike traditional methods that rely on self-sensing, this innovative technique incorporates both, enabling precise localization and quantification of delaminations in a carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) structure. By integrating both approaches, the limitations of self-sensing EIT are overcome, allowing for accurate identification of multiple damages and determination of their depth. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid method, with delaminations successfully detected and characterized with high accuracy.

This research paper delves into the concept of collective intelligence, examining the relationship between the cognitive abilities of individual team members and the overall performance of the group. By drawing on recent studies, we explore the counterintuitive phenomenon where groups composed of less competent individuals can outperform those made up of highly skilled individuals. We also investigate the underlying mechanisms behind this effect, considering factors such as group dynamics, diversity, and complementary skills. Ultimately, our analysis challenges the conventional wisdom that greater individual intelligence always translates to enhanced collective intelligence.

We present an innovative approach to learning optimal controllers for complex, high-dimensional systems using limited data. By leveraging optimal control theory and learning from optimal trajectories, our method enables rapid adaptation to new targets and efficient use of available information, including optimal state feedback and optimal cost-to-go. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to optimal control problems with various constraints, including linear dynamics and optimal control problems with limited data.

This study explores the relationship between geometric concepts and the tensor calculus for Euclidean spaces, highlighting the limitations of the latter and the potential for more efficient, geometrically informed approaches. The study also presents an alternative method for tensor differentiation, based on the concept of a geometric object, and demonstrates its benefits in reducing complexity and enhancing clarity.

We investigate a theoretical scenario where neutrally charged, light particles interact weakly with matter, yet experience an unexpectedly prolonged lifespan. These particles, which may have masses spanning from sub-electron volts to several hundred MeV, can persist for at least $10^{-9}$ seconds. We explore potential detection methods for these particles, which could be produced in significant quantities during the Big Bang, supernovae, or nuclear reactions. We also examine the possibility of these particles being created in laboratory settings, such as in particle accelerators, nuclear reactors, or radioactive sources. We find that their long lifespans can be achieved through a combination of weak interactions and a specific mass range, which can be produced in copious quantities while remaining detectable. We discuss potential detection methods for these particles, which could be produced in significant quantities during the Big Bang, supernovae, or nuclear reactions. We also examine the possibility of these particles being created in laboratory settings, such as in particle accelerators, nuclear reactors, or radioactive sources. We find that their long lifespans can be achieved through a combination of weak interactions and a specific mass range, which can be produced in detectable quantities while remaining consistent with current experimental constraints.

The COVID-19 pandemic forced a shift to remote learning, which significantly altered the educational experience for students.  Although remote learning provided flexibility and accessibility, it also presented challenges such as limited hands-on practice, technical difficulties, and a lack of social interaction.  As a result, the impact of remote learning on students' academic progress has been varied.  This study aims to investigate the effects of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track academically during the pandemic.  By collecting survey data from 100 students, this study found that remote learning had a negative impact on students' academic progress due to limited hands-on practice, technical difficulties, and a lack of social interaction.  However, the study also found that remote learning provided flexibility and accessibility, which helped some students stay on track academically.  The study's findings suggest that educators should provide more hands-on practice, technical support, and social interaction opportunities to help students stay on track academically during the pandemic.

This paper establishes the long-suspected Ward identities within the Toda conformal field theory, specifically for $\mathfrak{sl}_3$. By utilizing the known properties of Toda conformal fields, we derive these Ward identities, which can be applied to extract correlation functions from the theory.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess bi-automatic properties, thereby extending the earlier discovery that free products of bi-automatic groups with finite index subgroups are also bi-automatic.

This study investigates the thermodynamic behavior and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes influenced by a scalar field. The study reveals that adding a scalar field to the black hole can alter its thermodynamic stability, with certain parameter ranges allowing for a phase transition that can be triggered by varying the scalar field. The study also finds that the cosmic horizon can be eliminated by varying the scalar field, with the required change being minimal. The study's results suggest that the first law of black hole mechanics can be violated in the presence of a scalar field, with the required change in the scalar field being minimal. The study's findings have implications for the understanding of the cosmic censorship conjecture and the behavior of black holes in the presence of a scalar field.

This paper introduces four alternative versions of the ZFC axiomatic system,
utilizing paraconsistent and paracomplete logic. Specifically, we develop
axioms for set membership within the frameworks of the paraconsistent
ZF$\omega$-plus-C collection axiom, the paracomplete ZF$\omega$-plus-C axiom system,
the paraconsistent ZF$\omega$-plus-AC axiom of choice, and the paracomplete
ZF$\omega$-plus-AC axiom of choice.

This research focuses on a novel gait analysis technique that utilizes high-density electrocorticogram (ECoG) data to identify and analyze distinct phases of the walking cycle. By leveraging a machine learning approach, we developed a method to classify various types of walking movements and detect changes in step rates from ECoG data. Our approach involves training a machine learning model on a dataset of 100 participants, resulting in a highly accurate system capable of correctly identifying 95% of walking movements and step rates. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our technique by successfully detecting subtle differences in step rates as low as 0.1 Hz. Our research offers a non-invasive and precise means of monitoring and analyzing human locomotion, with potential applications in the fields of rehabilitation and sports medicine.

This paper proposes a new method to calculate entropy and related quantities, such as mutual information and Kullback-Leibler divergence, using nested sampling. Our approach leverages the nested sampling algorithm's ability to calculate the evidence, enabling us to determine entropy by evaluating the evidence of transformed probability distributions. We demonstrate our method with both analytical and numerical examples, including applications to cosmological data analysis.

We investigate the properties of right-angled Artin complexes, specifically those that admit a non-trivial geometric splitting, and establish a condition for a RAAC to have this property by analyzing its fundamental group.

Identifying how variables in a dynamic system interact is crucial for understanding complex systems. One effective method for analyzing these systems is Dynamic Efficient Connectivity (DEC), which maps the relationships between multiple time series variables. DEC is particularly useful in fields like neuroscience, where it can help study brain activity. However, existing DEC estimation techniques are computationally demanding, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. This study introduces a novel approach called Deep DEC Estimation (DDE), which utilizes a deep learning architecture to efficiently estimate DEC. DDE is capable of handling high-dimensional data and provides a computationally feasible solution for DEC estimation. Our results show that DDE outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency.

Phylogenetic networks are utilized in evolutionary biology to represent evolutionary histories that include complex events such as hybridization and gene flow.
To facilitate further investigation, researchers have developed various phylogenetic network generators to produce networks with specific characteristics.
These generators are often based on a particular distribution, and their effectiveness can be evaluated by comparing the structural properties of the resulting networks.
In this study, we assess several widely used phylogenetic network generators by analyzing the structural properties of the generated networks.
We find that these generators can be categorized into two groups: those that produce scale-free networks and those that do not.
We also explore the relationship between the parameters of the generators and the resulting network structures, and discuss the implications of our findings for the use of phylogenetic network generators in evolutionary biology.

Animals and plants exhibit various forms of movement, which can be observed through visual means. Understanding how they move is crucial for researchers in biology, ecology, and agriculture, as it sheds light on their behavior and interactions with their environment. This paper presents a computational approach to analyzing biological movement by using video footage. We discuss the challenges associated with this approach and present a range of techniques used to process video footage and extract movement data. We also explore the applications of this approach in different fields, including wildlife monitoring, crop protection, and veterinary medicine.

This paper introduces an innovative approach to solving large linear systems of equations, building upon higher-order methods that have been previously explored. A novel technique is proposed to expedite the convergence of an existing method, which is then compared to conventional approaches such as Gaussian elimination and LU decomposition. A Python-based implementation is developed and tested, with a focus on optimizing performance through parallel processing using GPU acceleration. A significant outcome of this research is the discovery that the proposed method can achieve a substantial reduction in computation time when dealing with large linear systems, with a notable improvement of up to 100 times faster than conventional methods.

Quantum scattering systems can be visualized as having a set of orthogonal pathways, or "eigenchannels," that a particle can take, each associated with a specific energy level. These channels are linked to a particular scattering matrix, or S-matrix, for a given energy level. We can define an "eigenchannel deposition" that measures the energy deposited in a specific channel, and this deposition can be thought of as the difference between the incident and scattered energies in that channel. We have derived a general rule for the cumulative eigenchannel deposition across all possible energy levels, and this rule is linked to the properties of the scattering system. We have also explored the implications of this rule for a specific type of scattering system, and found that it can be used to understand the behavior of these systems in a more intuitive way.

Building on the concept of topological Anderson insulators, our study focuses on one-dimensional systems with random binary disorders to explore their electronic properties. In contrast to previous research involving Gaussian distributed disorders, our findings reveal that certain types of random binary disorders can induce a topological phase within a previously stable insulating system. The phase transition point can be accurately predicted using a modified version of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, and our results demonstrate that this phenomenon occurs in a broad range of disorder strengths.

This paper explores the interplay between cuts and morphisms within the framework of linear logic, specifically highlighting how cuts can be eliminated through a combination of logical transformations. By leveraging the properties of the ! and ? modality, we demonstrate that any provable statement can be reduced to its fundamental components through a process of cut-free reasoning. This analysis is supported by the use of proof nets and their associated equivalence relations, which allow us to visualize the structure of complex logical arguments.

In a two-Higgs doublet model with complex parameters, the on-shell Higgs generation mechanism is examined, where the Higgs potential minimum occurs at zero phase for the neutral components of the two Higgs doublets, but with non-zero charged components. In this scenario, the CP-even and CP-odd components of the physical Higgs boson are massless, while the charged component is massive. The model's parameters are constrained by the requirement of a stable vacuum and the absence of charge instability. The model's predictions are analyzed in the context of the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, and the implications for the mass of the charged Higgs boson are discussed.

A linearity test for a network autoregressive model is proposed, which can be tested non-parametrically using a residual-based approach. The test's asymptotic properties are analyzed under both fixed and increasing network dimensions, and corresponding simulations are conducted to evaluate its performance. Additionally, a linearity test for a nonlinear network autoregressive model is developed and its properties are also examined.

This study focuses on problem-oriented approaches to neural network design, utilizing existing problem structures to guide the process. We examine two specific scenarios: the recovery of signals affected by noise and the resolution of partial differential equations. By leveraging the underlying framework of these problems, we can reduce the number of trainable parameters in our models, enhance their performance, and decrease computational costs.

A cell's interaction with its surroundings is heavily influenced by how it moves, disperses, and reorganizes its components, particularly proteins embedded in its membrane. This research proposes a versatile computational approach to model these processes, combining methods to simulate cell movement, membrane behavior, and protein relocation. The approach is demonstrated through various cell movement scenarios, including a moving particle model, a crawling cell model, and a more complex scenario involving a cell moving while also reorganizing its membrane. The reorganization of proteins is simulated using a simplified version of the Cahn-Hilliard equation, which is solved using a method that tracks proteins as they move across the cell's membrane. The results show that the approach can accurately simulate cell behavior in response to different stimuli and can be used to explore the underlying mechanisms driving cell movement and reorganization.

This study delves into the research of currency trails within blockchain networks, specifically in cryptocurrency networks. The research aims to shed light on the characteristics of the currency trails of suspicious activities, which can be utilized to identify and prevent illicit activities. The research methodology involves the analysis of the currency trails of suspicious activities in the Bitcoin network, which is the first of its kind. The research findings reveal that the average degree of the currency trails of suspicious activities is significantly lower than that of the overall network, which can be utilized to identify and prevent illicit activities. The research findings also reveal that the average path length of the currency trails of suspicious activities is significantly longer than that of the overall network, which can be utilized to identify and prevent illicit activities. The research findings have significant implications for the development of anti-money laundering systems and other security measures within blockchain networks.

NIST researchers have developed a reinforcement learning-based approach to enhance fault-tolerant quantum computation, specifically for the surface code. By training a codeword-based decoder using reinforcement learning, they achieved a significant improvement in logical error rates compared to the minimum-weight decoder, even when dealing with biased noise. The reinforcement learning decoder was found to be more robust to certain types of errors, particularly those caused by non-uniform error rates and decoder errors. The study also demonstrated that the codeword-based approach can be applied to other fault-tolerant quantum computing schemes, such as color codes and LDPC codes, and that it can be implemented on classical hardware.

In precision measurements, the maximum achievable sensitivity is determined by the total number of photons used in the process. This limit can be surpassed with the quantum-enhanced method, which involves preparing photons in a specific entangled state. A key challenge in this approach is the difficulty of generating and maintaining such a state. A proposed alternative method uses a two-cavity setup, where photons interact with atoms in each cavity and become entangled as a result of their interactions. This method offers a practical way to create photon-atom entanglement and, with further development, could enable improved measurements of the frequency and phase in optical systems. A key advantage of this method is its ability to achieve entanglement with a high degree of efficiency and robustness, even in the presence of technical noise.

The collaboration's measurements of particle associations between direct photons and hadrons in various collision types, including gluon-rich photons, isolated hadrons, and jet-hadron associations, are examined across different transverse momentum ranges and collision types. The findings are analyzed in the context of theoretical models of jet quenching and hadron production.

In this study, we introduce the concept of the sum of the Smarandache multiplication of digits, denoted as $\sigma(m!)$. The goal is to find the smallest natural number $n$ for which $\sigma(n!)$ equals $m!$.

Cloud computing's popularity has been driven by its ability to provide cost-effective computing resources, but the reliability of these resources is often compromised by network variability. This study investigates the impact of network fluctuations on large-scale applications, specifically examining how they affect resource utilization and performance. Through a combination of analytical modeling and real-world experimentation, we discovered that applications with significant variability in network efficiency can experience substantial performance degradation when scaled up. This degradation is exacerbated by the applications' tendency to become less efficient as they scale, leading to a phenomenon known as "noisy neighbor" effects. To mitigate this issue, we propose a new scheduling algorithm that takes network variability into account when allocating resources, resulting in improved performance and scalability for large-scale applications.

In a distributed contextual linear bandit setup, multiple agents operate in separate settings and aim to minimize cumulative regret by making optimal decisions based on their local context.
In this study, we examine a scenario where each agent has access to a unique context and only shares the context with other agents in the same setting.
We analyze a learning algorithm that enables agents to learn from their experiences and adapt to their local context, and we show that it achieves a cumulative regret bound of $O(d^{1/4}\sqrt{T\log T})$ per agent, and a total regret bound of $O(d^{1/4}\sqrt{NT\log T})$ across all agents.
We also consider a more challenging setting where each agent has access to a unique context and only shares the context with other agents in the same setting, and we show that it is possible to achieve a total regret bound of $O(d^{1/4}\sqrt{T\log T})$ in this scenario.

The transition to remote work has significantly impacted the effectiveness of agile methodologies, particularly Scrum, in various organizations.
This research combines survey data from 100 software development teams and case studies from 10 successful Scrum projects to examine the relationship between working from home and project success.
Our findings reveal that a higher prevalence of remote work correlates with lower project success rates, and this relationship is mediated by the successful execution of Scrum processes.
Furthermore, our results suggest that the impact of remote work on project success is influenced by team size, project duration, and the use of Scrum.
This research contributes to our understanding of the challenges associated with remote work and the implementation of agile methodologies, and offers practical guidance for managers seeking to improve project outcomes in remote work environments.

We appreciate the insightful feedback from the reviewers, which has significantly contributed to enhancing the clarity and accessibility of our research. In response, we have revised sections of the original manuscript to address these concerns. Specifically, we have modified the abstract, provided an expanded overview of the key findings, and included supplementary details on the data and experiments.

This study investigates the impact of event shape engineering on inclusive spectra and elliptic flow in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. By selecting events with enhanced or reduced average elliptic flow through event shape manipulation, we find that the resulting inclusive spectra for charged hadrons and multi-particle correlations exhibit a significant dependence on the event shape. Notably, the difference in $v_2$ between selected events with enhanced and reduced flow is comparable to that observed in events with normal flow. Furthermore, event shape manipulation has a minimal effect on the charged hadron spectra. In contrast, the $v_2$ dependence on event shape is more pronounced for charged pions than for charged protons.

This paper introduces the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform (QLCST) and examines its fundamental characteristics. It also investigates the relationships between QLCST and other transform methods, such as the Fourier Transform (FT), Linear Canonical Transform (LCT), and Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT). To solve an inverse problem, the paper derives an inversion formula for QLCST. Additionally, it defines two types of indeterminacy principles specifically for QLCST.

In wireless networks, power control is an effective method to optimize performance by adjusting transmission power. This paper focuses on the GDoF capacity of a $K$ user interference network and demonstrates that optimal power control can provide a significant benefit of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ over binary power control as $K$ increases. This finding is achieved through two key results: an upper bound of $O(\sqrt{K})$ GDoF gain for binary power control, and a direct binary power control scheme offering an $ \Omega(\sqrt{K})$ DoF gain over uncontrolled networks. The upper bound is established by proving the DoF gain of optimal power control is $ \Theta(K^{2/5}) $, and the $\Omega(\sqrt{K})$ gain result is established through the aforementioned binary power control scheme.

In particle simulations, a common issue is the significant disparity between the time scales of fluid and particle motion. To address this, researchers typically employ a small Courant number for the particle phase to allow for larger time steps. However, this approach can lead to unrealistic particle dynamics and reduced accuracy. An alternative method involves using a time step determined by the particle-particle collision frequency, which can result in more accurate simulations with only a minor reduction in time step size. This study demonstrates that using a physically determined time step can yield better accuracy than the conventional method of artificially increasing the particle relaxation time, and that this approach can be applied to simulations with a wide range of particle-to-fluid time scale ratios.

This article provides a comprehensive examination of the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$, where $n$ is a positive whole number. Initially, we explore the equation's solutions modulo various prime numbers, and subsequently, we investigate its whole number solutions by analyzing the equation's factorization within the ring of Eisenstein integers.

This paper presents a mathematical model of a hopping robot moving on a viscoelastic surface, along with a simulation model and an optimization approach for maintaining single-leg jumps. The surface is described using the Kelvin-Voigt framework, and the governing equations are solved using an indicator function to account for ground contact. A discrete energy-based control strategy is employed to develop an optimal control solution, which is then applied to a two-leg robot through a coordination control method.
In the flexible meson flexible scheme (MFS), we've developed flexible meson form factors, utilizing a flexible weight function and a flexible meson vertex within this model.

The phenomenon of electrohydrodynamics, which involves the application of electric fields to fluids, has been extensively studied in recent years. Researchers have extensively investigated this field in various applications, including the production of polymer films and inks, as well as in droplet-based technologies. In this study, we present an in-depth analysis of a previously observed phenomenon, known as the EHD fan, which occurs when a charged droplet is suspended in a gaseous medium. By employing high-speed imaging and laser-induced fluorescence, we have been able to visualize and measure the movement of the gas surrounding the droplet, revealing the formation of a rotating fan-like structure. Our findings provide new insights into the underlying mechanisms driving this phenomenon, as well as its potential applications in various fields.

To test large language models' ability to handle negation and double negation, we created a new dataset called CONDAQA, which is based on the SQuAD 2.0 dataset. We manually added negation and double negation questions to 1,000 SQuAD 2.0 passages, resulting in a total of 4,000 question-answer pairs. When we tested various baselines, we found that the current state-of-the-art model failed to accurately process negation and double negation questions, even though it performed well on the original SQuAD 2.0 dataset. Our results suggest that there is still room for improvement in handling negation in natural language understanding.

The concept of hierarchical organization is widely applied in various fields, including biology, linguistics, and social sciences. However, traditional methods for extracting hierarchical structures from diverse networks have limitations in scalability and efficiency. To address these challenges, we developed a scalable framework for computing hierarchies in diverse networks, consisting of three key components: a computationally efficient algorithm for identifying community structures, a method for extracting meaningful features from these structures, and a framework for analyzing the resulting hierarchical data. To demonstrate the scalability of our approach, we applied it to diverse networks, including the World Wide Web, citation networks, and social networks. Our results show that our framework can efficiently extract hierarchical structures from diverse networks, and that these structures are consistent with established methods for analyzing community structures.

Quantum annealing's effectiveness is influenced by the duration of the process, 
which can be viewed as a blend of adiabatic evolution and quench dynamics. 
Our study focuses on the quantum annealing process' characteristics during 
a finite time, specifically examining the exact cover problem. 
By analyzing the system's energy and entanglement entropy, 
we identify the presence of quench dynamics and its impact on the system. 
Our findings suggest that the system's behavior is determined by the 
relative speed of the quantum annealing process and the time it takes for 
the system to transition between different energy states.

Conformance checking is typically done by comparing a process model with an actual process execution derived from a process log. This comparison is often complicated by discrepancies between the process log and execution due to variations in how the process is performed. To address this, researchers have developed methods to identify a continuous segment of a process log that conforms to a process model, known as the maximal alignment problem. This paper presents an approach to solving this problem by utilizing infix and postfix alignments, which involves breaking down the problem into smaller, more manageable parts. Our approach is based on a precise definition of process alignments and their corresponding costs, which is then used to develop an algorithm for finding the best process log alignment with a specified definition of cost. This algorithm is then applied to conformance verification for process log executions, which is typically an NP-complete problem. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in verifying the conformance of trace fragments in a process log.

We have developed a two-band model for infinite-layer nickelate that accounts for the two distinct Fermi surfaces, and through the application of the Hubbard U model, we have demonstrated that this model can accurately reproduce the observed phase diagram, including the superconducting state. By utilizing the $T$-matrix approximation, we have found that a screening mechanism can explain the emergence of the gap in the smaller Fermi surface, and that this screening is most effective at intermediate to high doping levels, which is consistent with experimental observations.

This study investigates the long-term behavior of the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in an unbounded space, considering a hard sphere collision kernel and initial data that deviates slightly from a stable Maxwellian distribution. We demonstrate that, under these conditions, the phase blending effect, where particles collide and mix, dominates over the dispersion effect, leading to rapid convergence to equilibrium for high rates of dispersion. This holds true for a wide range of polynomial deviations from the hard sphere kernel, including the hard potential kernel, and applies to the entire space $\mathbb{R}^3$.

The Cox and Munk theory, originally formulated in 1954, has long been a cornerstone for understanding how the sea reflects light, and it has been extensively used in various fields such as remote sensing and weather forecasting. In this study, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of Cox and Munk wave statistics using a unique dataset consisting of 1.5 million infrared measurements from the IASI instrument on the Metop satellite. By combining this dataset with a numerical model of sea surface waves, we have been able to validate the Cox and Munk theory and explore its limitations in greater detail. Our findings reveal that the theory holds true for a wide range of sea conditions, but also highlights discrepancies between observed and predicted wave characteristics at higher wind speeds. These discrepancies may be attributed to the influence of breaking waves and other complex interactions between the sea and the atmosphere. Overall, our research provides valuable insights into the nature of sea surface waves and their impact on the reflection of light.

To optimize test case selection efficiency in software systems testing, an enhanced version of a specific test case choice algorithm is developed, featuring a parallelized singular value decomposition method. This improvement is demonstrated through a test case selection algorithm for software systems testing, where a singular value decomposition-based parallel algorithm is proposed for test case choice. The proposed algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness are validated through experimental results, showing significant performance gains in terms of execution time and test case coverage compared to existing sequential and parallel algorithms.

The global pandemic of COVID-19 has significantly impacted the world, causing widespread fear and uncertainty. Social media platforms have become a primary source of information, with users sharing their experiences and opinions on the pandemic. This study focuses on sentiment analysis of microblogging datasets related to COVID-19, aiming to classify posts as positive, negative, or neutral. We examined 10 pre-existing datasets and 1 new one, comparing various machine learning algorithms to determine the most effective approach. Our results indicate that combining multiple algorithms through ensemble techniques yields the best performance, achieving up to 90.1% accuracy. We also provide a comprehensive overview of the analyzed datasets and their characteristics, contributing to the field of sentiment analysis during times of crisis.

A modified version of the interlayer tunneling model, initially proposed by Davis and Zhang in 1996, has been developed to incorporate the effects of one-dimensional charge density waves in the CuO2 planes. This update reveals that the tunneling energy spectrum can be explained by considering only the interaction between electron and hole pockets within the CuO2 Fermi surface, while charge density wave effects can be attributed to the interaction between these nested pockets and the flat bands of the adjacent layer. Furthermore, this generalized model suggests that the tunneling spectra of cuprate superconductors exhibit similarities to those of charge density wave materials, such as Bi-based cuprates, which exhibit coexisting superconductivity and charge density wave states.

Theoretical models predict that the internal composition of massive stars may include strange quark matter, which could potentially be the same as the ground state of visible matter. This implies that the sound speed within the star's interior would be equal to the sound speed in the nuclear and strange quark matter states. The implication is that the presence of strange quark matter in a star's interior would result in a sound speed that is constant throughout, which would in turn affect the maximum mass of the star. The effect of a constant sound speed on the maximum mass of the star is significant, and it would be possible to distinguish this from a star with a soft equation of state by observing the star's gravitational waves.
